_comment: Ahmed's pre-approved opinion bank for the takes stream (config/takes.md). Each entry's `take` is the BELIEF (thesis), not post copy: the routine develops a fresh angle every time. `note` = optional angle hints. Edited by Ahmed by hand; the routine only updates last_used/times_used. PUBLIC REPO: every entry must already be public-safe.

opinions.take: AI is labor, not software. The question is never 'how can AI help with this task', it's 'why is a human doing this task at all'.
opinions.note: Most AI pilots die because they aim at a 10% improvement of an existing workflow instead of replacing it.

opinions.take: A chatbot improves a workflow. An agent replaces it. That gap is the whole difference between an AI feature and an AI business.
opinions.note: Inputs, process, feedback loop, scale: think in systems, not features.

opinions.take: Pick models like an electrician picks wire gauge: by cost-per-task math, not leaderboards or brand loyalty. Most teams are overpaying for intelligence their task doesn't need.
opinions.note: Treat LLMs as plumbing. Benchmark worship is the new framework worship.

opinions.take: The skill of the decade isn't prompting, it's verification. Don't trust any output, including your own agents', without checking it.
opinions.note: The people who get burned by AI are the ones who stopped auditing.

opinions.take: Most people use AI like Google. The unfair advantage goes to those who use it like an employee: brief it, delegate, review its work, fire the approach that underperforms.
opinions.note: Search engine vs workforce. Subtle difference, completely different outcomes.

opinions.take: AGI debates are entertainment. The operative questions are: can it cut cost, save labor, or make revenue this quarter. AI is an economic event before it's a philosophical one.
AI gives you leverage, and leverage amplifies whatever you point it at. Pointing it at eight things gets you eight mediocre outcomes. Focus got MORE important when the tools got powerful, not less.
opinions.note: Honest self-critique angle works: the challenge is never lack of ideas, it's choosing the one that deserves 12 months.

opinions.take: Automation can scale a sales motion that already works. It cannot find product-market fit for you. Early on, founder-led selling beats any outreach machine you can build.
opinions.note: Credible because Ahmed builds outreach machines and still says this.

opinions.take: AI is a great sparring partner for big decisions, but AI pushback is not customer pushback. One real user trying your product teaches you things no model conversation will.
Building from Pakistan for global markets is an advantage, not an apology. Geography gives you a cost base and a hunger most competitors don't have.
opinions.note: Arbitrage is a lens, not a limitation. Aim up, never self-deprecating.

opinions.take: Hiring is the most automatable white-collar workflow that still mostly runs on vibes. Resumes, screens, interviews, scoring: it's a pipeline, and pipelines can be instrumented.
opinions.note: Earned territory (Ahmed builds in hiring). Never cite internal Ployo specifics.

opinions.take: The model is not the moat. Whoever owns the workflow owns the customer; the model underneath gets swapped like a part.
Ship the ugly version this week. A broken demo in front of a real user teaches more than a month of planning. Iteration speed is the only durable advantage small teams have.
Everything finally looks buildable, which makes saying no the scarcest founder skill of the AI era. The constraint moved from 'can we build it' to 'should this consume the next 12 months'.
Memorizing facts without the mechanism behind them is renting knowledge. Understand why something happened once and you stop needing to memorize ten things that happened.
opinions.note: Applies to learning AI tools too: mechanisms over recipes.

opinions.take: AI doesn't take jobs, it takes tasks. Jobs are bundles of tasks, and the rebundling is where the next decade of companies gets built.
opinions.note: Future-of-work is earned territory.

opinions.take: Agents in production are 10% intelligence and 90% plumbing: retries, logging, guardrails, kill switches, audit trails. The hard part was never the model.
Treat constraints as design parameters, not obstacles. A hard limit you respect early produces a better system than freedom you have to clean up later.
The 10-person company running a 100-agent workforce is coming, and it will out-execute the 200-person company holding meetings about AI adoption.
Never give an agent a capability you can't audit. Autonomy without a kill switch and a log isn't leverage, it's liability with good marketing.
The highest-value prompt is 'tell me why I'm wrong'. People who ask AI for answers get average answers. People who ask it for pushback get better thinking.
Optionality feels like safety and bills you in focus. Every hedge you keep open costs you compounding on the main bet. Hedging is a tax: sometimes worth paying, never free.
opinions.note: Keep generic; never reference Ahmed's actual personal hedges.

opinions.take: Stop doing tasks; build the machine that does them. If something takes 10 hours by hand, the move isn't doing it faster, it's making it a 1-hour system.
opinions.note: Leverage hates linear effort.

opinions.take: Playing with new AI tools is a hobby. Folding them into production the week they ship is a career. Being 12 months ahead in HOW you use AI compounds harder than any single product you build.

Time-to-hire is the wrong number to chase. The metric that actually bleeds you is time-to-no: how long a candidate waits to find out they're a dead end. Most pipelines optimize the offer and ignore the 90% who get strung along.
opinions.note: Contrarian against the time-to-hire orthodoxy. The fast rejection is a feature, not a failure. Builder-in-the-arena framing.

opinions.take: The ATS isn't broken. It's doing exactly what we asked: filter on keywords, not capability. We built a machine to count nouns and then act surprised it can't read a human being.
opinions.note: Reframe-the-villain. Critique the system design, never a named vendor. The problem is what we optimized it for, not the software.

opinions.take: A resume is a self-reported, retro-edited marketing document, and we've built the entire top of the funnel on it. It's the worst sensor in the whole pipeline and somehow the one we trust most.
opinions.note: First-principles: the resume as a low-fidelity signal. The interesting question is what replaces it as the primary signal, not how to parse it better.

opinions.take: Most interviews don't measure whether someone can do the job. They measure whether someone is good at interviews. Those are different skills, and we keep hiring for the second one.
opinions.note: Interview theater. Unstructured charisma-detection vs structured signal. Earned to say from the interview-builder seat.

opinions.take: Structured interviews predict performance roughly twice as well as the freewheeling chat most managers prefer, and rubrics cut bias hard. Yet we keep defending gut feel because it flatters the interviewer. Structure beats vibes, and the data has said so for decades.
opinions.note: Structure-beats-vibes with receipts (the validity gap is well-documented research, not a fabricated stat). The reason it isn't adopted is ego, not evidence. Pair with: this is why we built AI to enforce structure.

opinions.take: Ghosting candidates isn't rudeness, it's a capacity problem dressed up as one. A recruiter drowning in 800 applicants physically cannot reply to 780 of them. Either you automate the close-out or you keep blaming individuals for a math problem.
opinions.note: Reframes candidate ghosting as a systems failure, not a character flaw. Honest middle ground: automation's most defensible job is the rejection nobody has time to send. Candidate-experience lane WITH a mechanism, not a platitude.

opinions.take: I build AI screening and I'll say what my own category won't: it's genuinely good at consistency and genuinely bad at the exceptional outlier. The career-switcher, the unconventional path, the person whose best signal isn't on paper. If your AI screen has no human override for the weird-but-brilliant, you've automated mediocrity.
opinions.note: The honest-vendor confessional. Owns the 'I'll tell you what my own category hides' seat. Human-in-the-loop spine. Specific-but-unverifiable builder candor.

opinions.take: Chasing candidates who use AI mid-interview is a losing arms race. The smarter move is to design interviews where using AI in the moment doesn't help: probing follow-ups, reasoning under pressure, 'why did you do it that way'. If a co-pilot can ace your interview, the problem is your interview.
opinions.note: Designing-for-AI-vs-AI whitespace. Direct from the interview-builder seat. Contrarian against the 'detect the cheater' crowd. The fix is interview design, not surveillance.

opinions.take: If your hiring AI can't tell a candidate why they were rejected in plain language, you don't have a product, you have a black box that happens to make decisions about people's livelihoods. Explainability isn't a compliance checkbox. It's the difference between a tool and a verdict machine.
opinions.note: Transparency-as-a-product-stance whitespace. The trust high-ground the black-box vendors can't take. Explainable + bias-aware spine. Stake a flag without naming a competitor.

opinions.take: AI doesn't remove hiring bias, it scales whatever bias is in the data you trained it on. Feed it ten years of biased human decisions and you get a faster, cheaper, more confident version of the same discrimination. The honest claim isn't 'unbiased AI', it's 'AI we actively audit for bias'.
opinions.note: Bias-aware spine, the responsible-builder line. Directly counters the lazy 'AI is objective' pitch. The cautionary-tale framing (models learning from biased human decisions) is the credible flag to plant.

opinions.take: Human-in-the-loop is quietly going from best practice to legal requirement. Regulators are converging on the same idea: a machine can assist a hiring decision, but a human has to own it. Founders treating that as red tape are about to get a very expensive lesson; the ones who built it in are about to get a moat.
opinions.note: Regulation-for-operators whitespace (EU AI Act high-risk classification, NYC LL144, state disclosure laws, converging without naming a fabricated deadline). Operator-facing, not legalese. Compliance as moat, not chore.

opinions.take: The AI-hiring discourse obsesses over engineering roles while ignoring where the volume actually is: care, health, frontline, hourly. One office job gets 40 applicants and a careful human read. One frontline role gets 800 and a coin flip. That's where screening is most broken and most worth fixing, and almost nobody serious is building for it.
opinions.note: Volume-screening-done-right whitespace. AU aged-care/health is a proof point, NEVER the boundary, frame as an underserved global segment. Contrarian against the white-collar-obsessed discourse.

opinions.take: When AI eats sourcing and first-round screening, the recruiter job doesn't shrink, it moves up the stack. The work that's left is the work that always mattered: judgment on the close calls, selling the role to a great candidate, advising the hiring manager who's wrong. The admin was never the job. We just confused being busy with being valuable.
opinions.note: Tasks-not-jobs applied specifically to the recruiter role, sharper than the saturated version. The recruiter becomes the closer/advisor, not unemployed. Respectful to the audience while still contrarian.

opinions.take: Every CEO now wants 'AI-fluent' hires and almost no one can define what that means or test for it. It isn't knowing prompt tricks. It's whether someone can delegate to a model, catch where it's confidently wrong, and verify the output. Until TA can measure that, 'AI fluency' on a job ad is a wish, not a screen.
opinions.note: Measuring-AI-fluency whitespace, the field has the demand and no validated method. Builder who scores candidates can credibly propose what the real signal is (delegate, catch errors, verify). Ties to verification-is-the-skill.

opinions.take: AI is eating the exact entry-level tasks that juniors used to learn the job on. Screening, drafting, first-pass research, the grunt work that was secretly an apprenticeship. If we automate the bottom rung, we have to consciously rebuild how people get their first shot, or we run out of seniors in a decade. This is a design problem, not a thing to mourn.
opinions.note: First-rung-crisis from the hiring-mechanics angle, NOT 'AI kills jobs' doom. Founder-of-hiring-tech is placed to own the rebuild question. Forward-looking, names a real second-order risk without fabricating numbers.

opinions.take: Hiring teams still act like they're the only ones evaluating. The candidate is screening your company the whole time: your reply speed, your interview competence, whether a human ever showed up. In a market where good people have options, a sloppy hiring process isn't just inefficient, it's a public referendum on how you'll treat them once they're inside.
opinions.note: Candidate-experience lane reframed as a two-way evaluation with stakes for the employer. The process IS the employer brand. Avoids the bare 'be human' platitude by tying it to a concrete consequence (losing the people you most want).
